title: Muse Spark Open: Meta's 816B Open-Weight Model
description: Muse Spark Open is Meta's 816B/42B-active open-weight coding model with a 1M context. Specs, benchmarks, pricing, and how to run it.
author: freellm.site
content:
**Muse Spark Open is the open-weight release of Meta's Muse Spark agentic coding model, published on October 15, 2026 by Meta Superintelligence Labs under the Muse Model License.** It's a sparse mixture-of-experts transformer with 816B total parameters and 42B active per token, a 1M-token context window, and native text, image, audio and video input. You can download the checkpoint from Hugging Face or use it through hosted providers including OpenRouter, Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten, Groq, Modal and Nebius.

![Muse Spark Open: Meta's 816B Open-Weight Model](/images/blog/muse-spark-open-meta-guide/image-0.jpg)

## What Muse Spark Open is

Muse Spark Open is the open-weight sibling of the Muse Spark models Meta has shipped through its API all year (Muse Spark 1.1 in July, 1.3 in September). The [model card](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B) describes it as "an 816B total/42B active parameter open weights model with a context window of 1M tokens," built for coding and agentic work and natively multimodal. Meta's research blog calls it [the most capable US open-weight model to date](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-spark-open).

The architecture, per the model card and the [Hugging Face launch post](https://huggingface.co/blog/meta-muse-spark-open):

| Property | Muse Spark Open |
| --- | --- |
| Parameters | 816B total / 42B active per token |
| Type | Mixture-of-Experts transformer + Perception Encoder |
| Experts | 256 per MoE layer, 8 selected per token |
| Layers / hidden dim | 62 / 8192 |
| Attention | 128 query heads, 16 KV heads (GQA), head dim 64, QK-norm |
| Context length | 1M tokens at inference |
| Vocabulary | 202,048 |
| Inputs / outputs | Text + image + video + audio in; text out |
| Languages | Data from 100+ languages |
| Checkpoints | BF16 and NVFP4 (AMD also released MXFP4) |
| License | Muse Model License (limited commercial terms) |
| Release date | October 15, 2026 |

Two things stand out. First, the sparsity: you load 816B parameters into memory but pay only 42B worth of compute per token, which is why hosted throughput is competitive with much smaller dense models. Second, according to the [vLLM day-0 post](https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-15-muse-spark-open), Muse Glimmer 30B was distilled from this model. If you've been running Glimmer locally, Spark Open is its teacher, and the two share a tokenizer and chat template.

### What Meta says it's good at

The model card lists seven target uses: multi-step reasoning, completing agentic tasks end to end, coding agents, tool use across long multi-turn workflows, multimodal reasoning over screenshots, charts and recordings, synthetic data generation, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Meta's own demos ran agentic workflows entirely on-device, shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame.

## Benchmarks from the model card

Meta published head-to-head numbers against other large open-weight models, using xhigh reasoning effort, temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0 and top_k disabled. Selected rows:

| Benchmark | Muse Spark Open | Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B | GLM 5.3 | Kimi K3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index | 39 | 40 | 45 | 44 |
| JobBench | **61.8** | 52.7 | 61.4 | 54.3 |
| MCP-Atlas | **89.2** | 84.5 | 84.2 | 82.3 |
| OSWorld Verified | 80.4 | — | — | 84.8 |
| Toolathlon Verified | 72.8 | 72.5 | 73.0 | 76.5 |
| HLE-Diamond (no tools) | **26.1** | 17.3 | 16.4 | 22.2 |
| AA Omniscience | **25** | 4 | 14 | 20 |
| GPQA Diamond | 89.0 | 93.5 | 91.7 | 93.5 |
| DeepSWE 1.1 | 60 | 57 | 67 | 68 |

Muse Spark Open leads on tool-calling and agentic benchmarks (MCP-Atlas, JobBench) and on knowledge without tools (HLE-Diamond, AA Omniscience). GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 are ahead on the raw coding benchmark (DeepSWE 1.1) and the general intelligence index. Meta calls the model "coding-optimized," but "agent-optimized" describes these results better. The full methodology is in Meta's [evaluation methodology report](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-spark-open); for anything not in the table, check the official docs rather than trusting a secondhand number.

## Running it: hosted vs self-hosted

The [developer docs](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-spark-open) describe two paths.

### Hosted via an OpenAI-compatible gateway

For most people this is the realistic option. OpenRouter lists Muse Spark Open at **$1.25 / $4.25 per 1M input/output tokens** with a 1M context, served by Modal, Together, Nebius Token Factory, Fireworks and Baseten, all at the same posted price, with $0.15/M cache reads at most providers. Thanks to cache hits, OpenRouter's page shows a weighted average input price of **$0.5127/M**, and the best provider (Baseten) has a P50 throughput of 237 tok/s. See the [OpenRouter model page](https://openrouter.ai/meta/muse-spark-open) for live numbers.

The gateway speaks the OpenAI schema, so calling it is a base-URL swap, the same pattern covered in [What Is an OpenAI-Compatible API and How to Use One](/blog/openai-compatible-api-guide/):

```python
from openai import OpenAI
import os

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"],
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="meta/muse-spark-open",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a careful refactoring agent."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "Find the N+1 query in this file and fix it."},
    ],
    temperature=1.0,
    top_p=1.0,
    extra_body={"reasoning_effort": "xhigh"},
)

print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

Note `reasoning_effort`. Meta recommends temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0, top_k disabled, and `reasoning_effort` set to `low`, `medium`, `high` or `xhigh` (default `xhigh`). Use `high`/`xhigh` for complex problem solving, coding and agentic tasks, and `low`/`medium` for faster, shorter responses; any other value returns an error. Output tokens are the expensive side at $4.25/M, so reasoning effort is the main way to control cost.

### Self-hosting

The hardware requirements are steep. According to the docs, the BF16 checkpoint is about 1.65 TB of weights and serves on eight GPUs such as 8 × B300, and the NVFP4 checkpoint is about 537 GB and serves on a single 4-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell node. Budget roughly 2 TB of VRAM for BF16 once you include KV cache, activations and runtime overhead. The model card gives minimums of 700 GB VRAM for NVFP4 and 2 TB for BF16.

Supported runtimes are SGLang, vLLM, Hugging Face, TensorRT-LLM, Unsloth and llama.cpp. vLLM shipped day-0 support with prebuilt images (`vllm/vllm-openai:muse-spark-open` for NVIDIA, `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:muse-spark-open` for AMD) and this serve command:

```bash
export VLLM_USE_RUST_FRONTEND=1

vllm serve meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 \
    --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
    --enable-expert-parallel \
    --max-model-len 1048576 \
    --reasoning-parser muse \
    --tool-call-parser muse \
    --enable-auto-tool-choice
```

vLLM also trained a DSpark draft model for speculative decoding on CUDA and ROCm. Meta's release notes mention custom auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang with kernel-level speedups of 1.03× to 3.95× on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

There's also an unusual option: Meta optimised Muse Spark Open for Apple silicon via MLX and says two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra can hold the whole model, since the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU can use up to 512 GB of unified memory per machine at 1.2 TB/s. That puts a frontier open-weight model on a desk, about as far as local inference goes. The [MLX adapter](https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx-lm) pulls weights straight from Hugging Face.

The Hugging Face repo is **gated** (the repository's conditions require manual approval), and the weights come in BF16 and NVFP4. For fine-tuning, Meta points to PyTorch's TorchTitan; see the [PyTorch announcement](https://pytorch.org/blog/muse-spark-open/).

## Is there a free way to try it?

Not from Meta directly. The open-weight release is weights plus third-party hosting, and the launch partners are paid inference providers and cloud model catalogs (Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Microsoft Foundry), with OpenRouter as the gateway. Some gateways offer promotional or trial credits from time to time, so check each provider's current terms.

If your budget is zero, prototype your agent loop on a free tier and switch the model string to `meta/muse-spark-open` once the scaffolding works. Our roundups of the [best free LLM APIs for coding in 2026](/blog/best-free-llm-apis-for-coding/) and the [drop-in OpenAI-compatible free list](/blog/openai-compatible-free-llm-apis-list/) cover which free endpoints handle tool calling well enough to stand in. If the 1M context is your main reason for wanting Spark Open, compare it with [free APIs with the largest context windows](/blog/free-llm-api-largest-context-window/) before paying per token. When you're ready to price the paid tier, [how to compare costs after the free tier](/blog/cheapest-llm-api-after-free-tier/) explains the input/output price gap, which matters a lot for a model whose output costs 3.4× its input.

## Safety, license, and the agent-liability question

Meta added safety post-training specifically for the open-weight version "to make it more robust against misuse as a standalone model without system guardrails," and recommends deploying it inside a larger AI system with guardrails suited to the use case. For agentic deployments the model card goes further: require human confirmation for irreversible actions, don't expose raw chain-of-thought in user-facing apps, protect internal assistant messages from user manipulation, and layer defences against jailbreaks.

Take that advice seriously. A model that plans, calls tools and corrects itself over long tasks takes actions with real consequences, and the law on who answers for those actions is still being written; see [FTC: AI Developers Liable for Their Agents' Conduct](/blog/ftc-ai-agent-liability-developers/) and [Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Breaks the Law?](/blog/who-is-liable-when-ai-agents-break-the-law/). If you self-host open weights, the deployment and its guardrails are yours, and no vendor moderation layer sits between your agent and production.

The license is the Muse Model License, with "limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free," plus an Acceptable Use Policy. "Many developers" isn't "all developers," so read the license text before you build a product on it.

## How it compares

| | Muse Spark Open | Muse Spark 1.3 (API) | Muse Glimmer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weights | Open (gated download) | Closed, API only | Open, small dense |
| Architecture | 816B MoE / 42B active | Not published as open | Dense |
| Local run | Yes, with 700GB+ VRAM or 2× M5 Ultra Macs | No | Yes, consumer-friendly |
| Multimodal in | Text, image, video, audio | Multimodal | Image/text perception |

If you want frontier agentic capability with weights you control, pick Spark Open and accept the hardware cost. If you want the same family without running infrastructure, the hosted Muse Spark 1.3 endpoint is on [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/meta/muse-spark-1.3). If you want something that runs on a laptop, Muse Glimmer is the distilled student. Before committing to any of them for daily coding, think about how you'll evaluate agentic coding models at all; [AI Engineer Interviews: How to Test AI-Assisted Coding](/blog/ai-engineer-interview-ai-assisted-coding/) has a framework that works for models as well as candidates.

## FAQ

### Who made Muse Spark Open and when was it released?

Meta Superintelligence Labs. The model card gives the release date as October 15, 2026, and the model provider as Meta Platforms, Inc. or Meta Platforms Ireland Limited.

### How many parameters does Muse Spark Open have?

816B total parameters with 42B active per token. It's a mixture-of-experts transformer with 256 experts per MoE layer and 8 routed per token. The Hugging Face repo lists the on-disk size as about 822B parameters including the Perception Encoder.

### Can I run Muse Spark Open on my own hardware?

Only with serious hardware. The docs specify roughly 537 GB of weights for NVFP4 (a single 4-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell node) or about 1.65 TB for BF16 (eight GPUs such as 8 × B300), with roughly 2 TB of VRAM budgeted for BF16 serving. Meta also optimised it for two Mac Studios with M5 Ultra using MLX. Supported runtimes include SGLang, vLLM, Hugging Face, TensorRT-LLM, Unsloth and llama.cpp.

### How much does Muse Spark Open cost through a hosted provider?

OpenRouter lists $1.25 per 1M input tokens and $4.25 per 1M output tokens, with $0.15/M cache reads at most providers, across Modal, Together, Nebius, Fireworks and Baseten. Prices change, so check the [OpenRouter model page](https://openrouter.ai/meta/muse-spark-open) or each provider's own pricing before you budget.

### Is Muse Spark Open free to use commercially?

It ships under the Muse Model License, with "limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free," plus a separate Acceptable Use Policy. Whether your use qualifies depends on the license text, so read the [license](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B/blob/main/LICENSE.md) and the usage policy directly, and check the official docs if anything is unclear.
